stem: Define headache (cephalgia), list the pain-sensitive structures of the cranium, and differentiate primary from secondary headaches.
options: Headache (cephalgia) is an unpleasant sensation in the cranial vault and below the orbits, spreading over the scalp to the occipital region. Pain-sensitive cranial structures are the venous sinuses, dura, cranial blood vessels, three divisions of CN V (trigeminal), CN VII (facial), CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), and the first three cervical nerves. Primary headaches (tension-type, migraine, cluster) have no associated organic cause, whereas secondary headaches stem from organic causes like brain tumour, aneurysm, or increased intracranial pressure.

The four phases are: (1) Prodromal Phase (irritability, depression, food cravings, anorexia, fluid shifts), (2) Aura Phase (visual flashes/spots, warmth, confusion, weakness from spreading oligemia moving occipital-to-frontal at 2–3 mm/min), (3) Headache Phase (4–72 hours of incapacitating throbbing pain with hibernation from stimuli), and (4) Recovery/Postdromal Phase (gradual cessation, neck/scalp tenderness, exhaustion, prolonged sleep). Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan) are first-line because they selectively target serotonin receptors, reduce neurogenic inflammation of cerebral blood vessels, and induce vasoconstriction.

stem: Define pain according to the IASP, list its five dimensions, and explain why the patient's self-report is central to pain assessment.
options: Nociceptive pain arises from tissue irritation or injury activating nociceptors (deep/superficial somatic or visceral), feels localized, aching, throbbing, or sharp, resolves with healing, and responds well to opioids. Neuropathic pain stems from peripheral or central nervous system injury/malfunction (e.g., diabetic peripheral neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain, carpal tunnel syndrome), feels burning, shooting, or electric shock-like with allodynia, is often chronic, and responds poorly to opioids alone, requiring adjuvant antidepressants or anti-seizure drugs.

The IASP defines pain as an unpleasant sensory sensation and emotional experience primarily associated with tissue damage or described in terms of such damage, or both. Its five dimensions are physiologic, affective, cognitive, behavioural, and socio-cultural. Because pain is purely subjective and cannot be objectively measured by laboratory tests, the patient's self-report is the single most reliable indicator of the pain experience.

During persistent stress, the hypothalamus secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), stimulating the pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which prompts the adrenal cortex to release glucocorticoids (cortisol, increasing blood glucose and modulating immunity) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, promoting sodium retention and potassium excretion), regulated by feedback loops. Three symptom-management drug classes are benzodiazepines (enhancing GABA calming signals), beta-blockers (blocking epinephrine and norepinephrine binding), and buspirone (balancing dopamine and serotonin for anxiety).

Eustress is short-term positive stress perceived as within coping abilities that excites, focuses energy, and improves performance, whereas distress is short- or long-term unpleasant negative stress exceeding coping abilities that impairs performance and health. Stress is the body's non-specific reaction to a stressor affecting all body systems, whereas adaptation is the adjustment process maintaining physiological, psychological, socio-cultural, intellectual, and spiritual homeostasis. SOC comprises Comprehensibility (events feel structured and predictable), Manageability (resources are available to cope), and Meaningfulness (demands are challenges worthy of engagement).

stem: Describe the distribution of body water across ICF and ECF compartments, explain why infants and older adults are at greater risk for fluid imbalance, and distinguish crystalloids from colloids.
options: FVD presents with tongue furrows, poor skin turgor, urine output <30 mL/hr, flat supine neck veins, weight loss (2–8%), orthostatic hypotension, and elevated Hgb, Hct, and urine specific gravity—managed by careful IV fluids, isotonic NG irrigation, oral care, and slow position changes. FVE presents with puffy eyelids, pitting edema (1+ to 4+), ascites, moist lung rales, bounding pulse, distended neck veins, high CVP, and decreased Hgb/Hct—managed by sodium restriction, diuretics, high Fowler's positioning, bed rest, daily weights, strict I&O, and abdominal girth monitoring.

Body water averages 60% of adult body weight—two-thirds resides in ICF (40% body weight) and one-third in ECF (20% body weight, comprising plasma, interstitial fluid, and specialized cavities). Infants have high body water (70–80%) while older adults drop to 45–55%, making both age groups more vulnerable to fluid disorders. Crystalloids contain small solute molecules that cross semipermeable membranes to expand both intravascular and interstitial spaces, whereas colloids (albumin, dextrans, hydroxyethyl starches) contain large molecules that stay intravascular and pull interstitial fluid inward via high oncotic pressure.

Acidosis is an excess of plasma H+ causing arterial pH <7.35, whereas alkalosis reflects excess bicarbonate or decreased carbonic acid (pH >7.45). Acid-base balance is regulated by chemical buffers (20:1 bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio), the respiratory system (CO2 excretion), and the renal system (HCO3- conservation and H+ excretion). Respiratory alkalosis results from CO2 loss via hyperventilation (CO2 <35 mmHg, HCO3- <22 mEq/L), whereas metabolic alkalosis results from bicarbonate gain or acid loss such as prolonged vomiting or NG suction (HCO3- >29 mEq/L).

Hypokalemia (serum K+ <3.5 mEq/L) causes paralytic ileus, shallow respirations, postural hypotension, decreased reflexes, and ST depression/inverted T/peaked U waves on ECG. Hyperkalemia (plasma K+ >5.6 mEq/L; >8.5 mEq/L often fatal) causes cramps, diarrhea, paresthesias, bradycardia, heart block, and tall narrow T waves with widened QRS.
